newsitem.title: USA: Health groups to cast skeptical eye on tobacco deal.
newsitem.headline: Health groups to cast skeptical eye on tobacco deal.

text.p: Leading public health groups are likely to cast a sceptical eye on the proposed tobacco settlement when they review it on Wednesday, public health officials said Monday.

So far, most public health groups have either criticised the proposal or said they are withholding judgment while they study it. Only representatives of the American Medical Association have spoken out in favour of it, and the AMA itself will study it further before adopting a formal position.
Public health groups will gather in Washington for the third time on Wednesday to consider the settlement proposal and other aspects of long-term tobacco control goals.

The meetings have been convened by former Food and Drug Administration Commissioner Dr. David Kessler and former Surgeon General Dr. C. Everett Koop, both of whom have criticised aspects of the settlement proposal.

The opinions of Koop and Kessler will carry weight in Congress, which would have to pass complex legislation to enact the $368 billion settlement reached on Friday by the tobacco industry and the 40 states suing it.
Kessler starts his new job at Yale University next month, and Koop is scheduled to have knee surgery this week, so they are likely to push for decisive steps at Wednesday's meeting.

Congressional leaders have said they are unlikely to take up the issue for at least a few months. One committee, the Senate Judicary Committee, has scheduled a hearing for this Thursday about the proposal, but no formal legislation is pending.

A key concern of public health groups is FDA regulation of nicotine. Although the settlement proposal recognises the FDA's authority, critics say the wording of the agreement will give cigarette makers a loophole.
Kessler said over the weekend the settlement could "impede" FDA's ability to regulate tobacco. "There are a lot of hurdles for the FDA, some impossible burdens," he said.

Under the proposal, the FDA could not curtail nicotine unless it can demonstrate that safer tobacco products will not create a black market for the unsafer products. Critics of the settlement point out that it is hard, if not impossible, to prove that something will not happen in the future.

Underscoring their concern, some public health activists pointed to an interview with BAT Industries president Martin Broughton that appeared in the Wall Street Journal Monday. He was quoted as saying he was not worried about FDA regulation. "It's an unlikely prospect," Broughton said. "The contraband part gives me the most comfort."

The American Heart Association and the American Cancer Society, both of which had endorsed the concept although not the specifics of a settlement, are both studying the agreement between the industry and the states suing it to see if it meets their goals. Neither has endorsed the deal.
"We're just not commenting until we review it," said Trish Moreis, a spokeswoman for the American Heart Association. She said that would take until at least July 11.

Other prominent groups, notably the American Lung Association, have been critical of the negotiations. Some public health and legal officials said many health groups were deeply concerned about the FDA language, even if they have not yet taken a public position on that.
An exception is former AMA president Dr. Lonnie Bristow, who was involved in the negotiations with the industry.

"I think it's a carefully crafted, balanced, integrated program" that would aim to reduce youth smoking, help existing smokers and "make the industry pay for the health problems it caused," he said by telephone Monday.
"Of course Congress must inspect it very very carefully. It will be my hope that they are not contemplating substantive changes," he said.
Congressional critics of tobacco have made clear that they hope to make the agreement tougher on the industry.
"There's going to be a lot of careful scrutiny," Sen. Paul Wellstone, a Minnesota Democrat, said Monday. He said that he could not back the settlement without some changes.
